title: The innkeeper (1203)
hook: Dominic stays up all night talking with an innkeeper who held other beliefs

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Franciscan day at home, and the end of three weeks with Francis. Your line was praise and simplicity.

An inn in Toulouse, in the south of France. It's late. Two travelers from Spain come in off the road: a bishop named Diego, on an errand for his king, and a priest of his cathedral, a Castilian named Dominic. They're tired. They want a bed. But Dominic gets talking with the man who runs the inn, and finds his host holds beliefs very different from his own. He could nod politely and go upstairs. He doesn't. Today, the conversation that, by tradition, started an order.
screen: `AN INN IN TOULOUSE, LATE.` → `TWO TRAVELERS FROM SPAIN.` → `DOMINIC DOESN'T GO UPSTAIRS.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Jordan of Saxony, who followed Dominic as head of his order and wrote down how it began. The innkeeper, Jordan says, belonged to the movement the Church called heresy and historians call the Cathars. They taught that the material world was not the good work of a good God, and they lived lives of hard self-denial that impressed their neighbors. So Dominic, in Jordan's telling, spent the whole night with his host, talking earnestly and warmly. Not shouting him down, not threatening: talking, listening, and talking again, until dawn. By morning, Jordan says, the man could not resist the wisdom and spirit of what he heard, and returned to the Catholic faith. Notice what the story chooses to remember. Not a crowd, not a church council. One man, one table, one long night. A line from the first letter of Peter fits. In the Douay-Rheims it asks believers to be "ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." The next verse says how: with modesty and fear. Tradition says that night planted something in Dominic. Before it, he was a canon praying in his cathedral's choir. After it, he wanted to spend his life explaining, patiently, to people who saw the world another way. That's what his order would be called: the Preachers.
screen: `JORDAN OF SAXONY TELLS IT.` · `A HOST WHO SAW THE WORLD ANOTHER WAY.` · `ONE TABLE, ONE NIGHT, UNTIL DAWN.` · `A LIFE OF PATIENT EXPLAINING.` · then, large: `READY ALWAYS TO SATISFY EVERY ONE THAT ASKETH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who sees the world very differently from you, about faith, politics or how to live, and picture sitting across a table from them late at night, with nowhere to be. Choose one question you'd ask, really wanting the answer, and notice what you'd have to set down to hear it: the need to win, the clock, the speech you've rehearsed; if you pray, pray for that person by name.
The innkeeper. The man who held other beliefs, and the night Dominic spent at his table, talking until dawn. Today's word.
Your line: all night talking. In the story, one patient night at one table is where the Preachers began. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Dominicans tell the story of the innkeeper as the seed of their order, and Dominican friars and sisters still give much of their lives to study, preaching and long conversations with people who hold other views.

Jordan's account paraphrased: Diego of Osma traveling on the king of Castile's business, with Dominic; their host in Toulouse a heretic; Dominic disputing with him through the night 'strenuously and fervently' until he brought him back to the faith. Confirm wording ('earnestly and with warmth'; 'could not resist the wisdom and the spirit').
Cathar belief summarized fairly and briefly: the material world not the work of the good God; lives of hard self-denial that impressed neighbors.
Dominic described as 'a priest of his cathedral' / 'a quiet canon' (canon regular, sub-prior of Osma). Confirm.
1 Peter 3:16 'with modesty and fear' is paraphrased; Douay-Rheims wording of 3:15 to confirm.
